fields.connection: Vる / V passive form (る) + がままに (言われるがままに)
examples: He ended up signing an expensive contract, doing just as the salesman told him.
On the weekend, I set off on a trip wherever my heart led me.
I'll try living by going with the flow, letting things take their course.
I revised the documents just as my boss instructed.
She said nothing, letting her tears flow.
Please state your opinions just as you think.
fields.explain:
With the passive: tends to carry a passive nuance, a lack of initiative, sometimes criticism (“doing whatever one is told”).
With the active: carries a free, poetic/literary nuance (心の赴くがままに／思うがままに).
More formal/literary than “〜ままに”.

～るがままに expresses “leaving it to…; just as…; exactly in line with that state/wish”. It has two directions:
• Active and free: acting on one's own will/feelings (思うがままに＝as one pleases).
• Passive and resigned: being led/pushed along by what others say/what happens (言われるがままに＝doing whatever one is told).
fields.notes:
• Often used in fixed phrases: 言われるがままに／流されるがままに／心の赴くがままに／思うがままに.
• The “が” in “がままに” adds emphasis to the sense of “just as…/leaving it to…”.
• Suited to expository writing, literature and reportage; in conversation, “ままに/とおりに” sounds more natural.
mistakes: Not using the passive form: “言うがままに” → lacks the nuance of “being made to”; “言われるがままに” is more natural.
Confusing the meaning with “〜のとおりに”: “がままに” carries a nuance of letting things be/exactly as the state is, not simply “following instructions”.
Dropping “に” when an object follows: 思うがまま意見を… → use 思うがままに意見を…
Used in formal contexts; in casual conversation it may sound too literary.

rows: Being led by the nose/letting others do as they like
<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>われるがままに<ruby>従<rt>したが</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>指示<rt>しじ</rt></ruby>どおりに<ruby>作業<rt>さぎょう</rt></ruby>する。
<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>従<rt>したが</rt></ruby>って<ruby>行動<rt>こうどう</rt></ruby>する。

examples: No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out of the classroom.
No sooner had he sat down than he fell fast asleep.
The moment the door opened, the children dashed outside.
The moment she saw his face, tears spilled from her eyes.
No sooner had my father come home than he turned on the TV.
The moment the alarm went off, everyone started to evacuate.
fields.explain:
Has a narrative nuance, more formal than ordinary conversation; creates a sense of decisiveness and surprise.
Not used for predicted future events; almost always in the past when recounting things that have happened.
Avoid using it with durative verbs (続く、待つ…) because they lack “immediacy”.
The second clause does not use the speaker's command/volition/suggestion (～なさい、～ましょう、～てください…)

• Main translation: “As soon as/The moment V, …”, emphasizing an extremely quick succession of two actions/events.
• Faster than ～とたん(に); has a written/narrative nuance, creating a sense of an “instant reflex”.
• The second clause describes an actual event, usually a behavior/change that happens immediately, sometimes surprisingly.
• The subject of the first clause and the second clause is usually the same person/thing; if different, a clear context is needed to avoid ambiguity.
• Not used for the speaker's volition, commands, invitations or desires.
• Often used with verbs marking a starting point: 見る、聞く、開く、立つ、座る、鳴る…
fields.notes:
• Some common combinations: 見るが早いか／聞くが早いか／開くが早いか — the action “springs” very sharply.
• When the two clauses have different subjects, state them clearly to avoid misunderstanding: 先生が入るが早いか、学生たちは静かになった。
• Works well in narratives/news captions to add vividness and a fast pace.
mistakes: Using a command/suggestion in the second clause → grammatically incorrect.
Choosing a durative verb for the first clause → loses the sense of “as soon as”.
Confusing it with ～たとたん(に): ～るが早いか uses V-る and has a stronger written nuance.
Putting a future conjecture in the second clause (“will…”) → not appropriate; use an event that has already happened.

rows: More formal; almost never used for volition/commands.
ベルが<ruby>鳴<rt>な</rt></ruby>るや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や、<ruby>皆<rt>みな</rt></ruby>が<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がった。
Mostly requires the same subject; emphasizes an immediately following action.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>るなり、<ruby>寝室<rt>しんしつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>った。
Uses V-た; usually something unexpected; less written.
<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>ったとたん、<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>くなった。
～かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと／～かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>ったら
Heightens the nuance of surprise; usually a subject different from the speaker.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと、すぐやんだ。
More conversational; the “immediacy” is weaker than ～るが<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>いか.
<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>着<rt>ちゃく</rt></ruby>いたとすぐ、シャワーを<ruby>浴<rt>あ</rt></ruby>びた。

examples: As soon as he entered the room, he let out a big sigh.
The moment she heard the voice on the phone, her expression changed.
(I) fell asleep the moment I sat down.
The moment the child saw his father, he ran up to him.
As soon as he learned the result, he broke into a smile.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes “immediacy” and an element of surprise/unpreparedness.
The following sentence is usually an action/sign of emotion that occurs instantly (叫ぶ,泣き出す,笑う,驚く…).
Avoid using it with the speaker's commands/intentions; it leans toward describing events that have happened.
The past tense is usually used in the second clause (～た／～てしまった／～出した).

• Expresses two events that occur in succession, almost simultaneously: “just as/the moment V, …”.
• Nuance: written language, more formal than ordinary conversation; often accompanied by a surprising, unexpected result.
• Restriction: Usually not used for repeated habits; suited to single, sudden events.
fields.notes:
• Vるなり has a slightly archaic/literary nuance; suitable for reading comprehension tests and essays.
• Avoid using it for the future/volition: × 着くなり、連絡します (use ～たら／～次第で instead).
• Many materials require the same subject; when the subjects differ, prefer other patterns such as ～や否や／～かと思うと.
mistakes: Changing the subject between the two clauses: × 先生が入るなり、学生は立った → use ～や否や／～かと思うと.
Using it for a habit: × 帰るなり、テレビを見る (for habits, use と/たら/といつも).
Using it for a command/volition: × 着くなり、電話して (unnatural; use ～たら／～次第に電話する).

rows: Usually the same subject; written nuance
ドアを<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けるなり、<ruby>叫<rt>さけ</rt></ruby>んだ
ベルが<ruby>鳴<rt>な</rt></ruby>るや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>した
Emphasizes speed; usually the same subject
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るが<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>いか<ruby>逃<rt>に</rt></ruby>げた
Emphasizes the unexpected; A is a moment
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたんめまいがした
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと<ruby>止<rt>や</rt></ruby>んだ

examples: It is no surprise that newcomers take their time.
His mistake does not deserve criticism.
There is no need to make a fuss over something like this. Let's stay calm and deal with it.
This success is nothing to praise, but the effort deserves recognition.
He is a victim too, so there is no reason to blame him.
fields.explain:
Used to tone down the degree of a reaction/evaluation: “one should not overreact”.
Common with verbs of evaluation/emotion:驚く,憤る,心配する,非難する,称賛する,絶賛する.
Usually comes at the end of a sentence or before から／ので to state a conclusion/a mild recommendation.

• Meaning: Not to the extent of having to…, not worth… (an evaluation that the degree is “unnecessary”).
• Two common directions of meaning:

Not worth being surprised at/criticizing/worrying about: 驚く・非難する・心配するにはあたらない。
Not worth excessive praise: 称賛するにはあたらない。

• Not worth being surprised at/criticizing/worrying about: 驚く・非難する・心配するにはあたらない。
• Not worth excessive praise: 称賛するにはあたらない。
• Nuance: Formal, objective, often used in commentary, news and reports.
fields.notes:
• Can be used as a modifier: 驚くにはあたらない出来事 (an event that is no cause for surprise).
• With nouns: 非難にはあたらない／称賛にはあたらない — common in legal documents and essays.
• The nuance is not prohibition, only “an evaluation that the degree is unnecessary”.
mistakes: Understanding it as “must not V”: incorrect. This is an evaluation of degree, not a prohibition.
Using it with concrete actions that involve no evaluation: × 走るにはあたらない (unnatural).
Confusing it with ～までもない: that pattern leans toward “no need to carry out the action”; ～にはあたらない leans toward “not worth reacting/evaluating that way”.

rows: <ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>するにはあたらない
<ruby>驚<rt>おどろ</rt></ruby>くほどのことではない
Not to the extent of having to do
Leans toward “no need to carry out the action”
<ruby>慌<rt>あわ</rt></ruby>てて<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>するまでもない
Written; means “no need” or “not as good as”
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>するには<ruby>及<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ばない

examples: I don't know his address or phone number. Even if I want to contact him, I don't know how.
It's my first time in this city and I don't know the way, so I have no idea even how to get to the station.
There isn't enough material, so I'm in no position even to write the report.
My computer broke, and even if I want to take it in for repair, there's no shop nearby.
With this budget, we don't have enough staff even to develop a new product.
There's no evidence, so even if I want to protest, I can't show any grounds.
fields.explain:
Pattern: Vる + にも + a clause expressing difficulty/lack of means/not knowing how.
Often used in written language and formal speech; natural when describing problems, in reports and mild complaints.
The subject is usually the speaker/the speaker's group; it does not express commands/requests.
The second clause avoids verbs of strong volition (〜ようと思う) unless stating “cannot/do not know”.

• Main meaning: “Even to V / when you want to V, … (it is still hard/there is no way/you don't know what to do)”. Used when lacking information or means, or facing objective obstacles.
• The “にも” nuance heightens the sense of helplessness and confusion: it puts the speaker in a situation of “wanting to do something but not knowing the way/being at a loss”.
• The second clause often contains: わからない, 見当がつかない, 困る, できない, 手段がない, 難しい, どうすればいいか.
• Describes a situation rather than volition; differs from the pattern of strong volition “Vようにも〜ない”.
fields.notes:
• After Vるにも, interrogative phrases are very typical: どうすればいいか, どこへ行けばいいか, 何をすべきか.
• In casual speech, the explanation can be partly omitted if the context is clear: 金がなくて、引っ越すにも…。 (sounds natural when the listener understands the rest).
• Do not confuse it with “どこへ行くにも” (wherever one goes) – this is “interrogative noun/pronoun + にも” meaning “also”, not the Vるにも pattern being studied.
mistakes: Mixing it up with “Vようにも〜ない” or “Vたくても〜ない”: note that the second clause of Vるにも is usually “not knowing how/lacking means”.
Using Vたにも… × (does not exist). It must be Vるにも…
A command/suggestion in the second clause is unnatural: × 行くにも、早く来てください。
Confusing it with “にもかかわらず”: the two patterns have completely different functions.

rows: Even to V, (it is hard/one doesn't know how)
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>うにも<ruby>手段<rt>しゅだん</rt></ruby>がない。
Want to V but cannot V
Stronger nuance of volition; a structure of its own
<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようにもできない。
Emphasizes “wanting” (feeling) rather than “how to do it”
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いたくても<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>えない。
In order to V / To V, …
Neutral, often used to evaluate conditions
Does not emphasize “not knowing how/lacking means”
<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>つからない。

fields.connection: Vる + にも + V potential form ない (泣くに泣けない)
examples: I'm so busy that I can't rest even if I want to.
The trains have stopped, so I can't go home even if I want to.
The tears won't come; I feel like crying but I can't.
With my boss right in front of me, it's the kind of atmosphere where I can't refuse even if I want to.
I'm feeling unwell, so I can't eat even if I want to.
The roads are closed, so we can't get to the venue even if we want to.
fields.explain:
Pattern: Vる + にも + the negative potential form of the same verb (or できない with サ変 verbs).
Emphasizes “the will is there but it is blocked”. Usually used in the first person, or to describe a general situation.
Nuance of lament and helplessness; more formal than VたくてもVられない.
The reason for the obstacle is usually stated before or after the sentence (with 〜ので/〜から/〜せいで/状況描写).

• Meaning: “Even if one wants to/intends to V, one cannot V” for objective reasons (busyness, circumstances, rules, suppressed feelings…).
• The structure emphasizes blocked volition: the first part states the “intention”, the second affirms “impossibility”.
• Pragmatics: complaining, explaining reasons, expressing a dilemma.
fields.notes:
• Typical, natural combinations: 泣くにも泣けない・笑うにも笑えない・休むにも休めない・帰るにも帰れない.
• Spoken language may use “ら抜き” (食べれない/来れない), but tests/JLPT prefer the standard forms 食べられない/来られない.
• A reason can come first: 事情があって、出席するにもできない。
mistakes: Wrong potential form: × 行くにも行かれない → it must be 行くにも行けない.
Confusing it with “Vるにも … (not knowing how)”: look at the second clause. If it is the negative potential of the same verb → pattern 167.
Using it with a command/suggestion is pragmatically wrong: × 行くにも行けないから、行け！
Dropping “も”: × 帰るに帰れない → in this pattern “にも” is mandatory.

rows: Emphasizes volition blocked by objective factors
<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>るにも<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>れない。
Even if one intends to V, one cannot
Strong nuance of volition; more written/emphatic
<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようにも<ruby>手段<rt>しゅだん</rt></ruby>がない。
Leans toward the personal feeling of “wanting”
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いたくても<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>えない。
Means “even having tried” rather than “want to but cannot”
<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>つからない。

examples: Charging an innocent person with a crime is an unforgivable act.
Falsifying data in research is a problem that must not be overlooked.
Disregard for human rights is a crisis that society must not overlook.
Trust is an indispensable quality in running an organization.
Fabricating historical facts is an unforgivable falsehood.
Compliance with safety standards is an indispensable requirement in manufacturing.
fields.explain:
Used to modify a noun, creating a sense of seriousness; formal, written language.
The meaning of prohibition/judgment (許すべからざる,容認すべからざる,許容すべからざる) and the meaning of necessity (欠くべからざる) must be distinguished by the verb.
Not used in everyday conversation; replace with ～てはいけない/～べきではない in spoken language.

• Meaning A (common): “Must not/should not V; V is unacceptable” → nuance of moral, legal or regulatory judgment.
• Meaning B (idiom): 欠くべからざる + N = “indispensable/essential” (the meaning is reversed by negating “欠く”).
• This is a classical form, used often in academic writing, serious journalism, political speeches and regulations.
fields.notes:
• Natural combinations: 許すべからざる罪/暴挙, 看過すべからざる事実/不正, 容認すべからざる差別, 忘却すべからざる教訓.
• With サ変 verbs, the form “すべからざる” is more common than “するべからざる”. Examples: 看過すべからざる, 容認すべからざる.
• In newspaper headlines, particles may be omitted for conciseness: “許すべからざる虚偽、明るみに”.
mistakes: Mistaking “indispensable” for the general meaning: it is only correct with 欠くべからざる.
Using it as an independent predicate: × これは許すべからざる。 → A noun is needed: 許すべからざる行為だ。
Using it in everyday conversation makes the sentence too stiff; replace with ～てはいけない/～べきではない.

rows: Archaic, very formal, modifies a noun
<ruby>許<rt>ゆる</rt></ruby>すべからざる<ruby>行為<rt>こうい</rt></ruby>
Modern norm, also used in imperative sentences
<ruby>差別<rt>さべつ</rt></ruby>してはならない。
<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をつくべきではない。
<ruby>欠<rt>か</rt></ruby>くべからざる<ruby>条件<rt>じょうけん</rt></ruby>

examples: Authorized personnel only. No entry.
No smoking here.
No photography within the temple/shrine grounds.
No illegal dumping of garbage.
Use of fire prohibited.
No talking during the exam.
fields.explain:
Used as an independent sentence (the subject is usually omitted), placed after a place noun or a noun indicating time/target.
For regulations, notices and signs; not used when speaking to someone face to face in everyday communication.
Can be accompanied by an adverbial phrase:当駅構内での飲酒、 厳禁 ／飲酒 するべからず。

• Prohibition: “Must not V”. Used on prohibition signs, in regulations and serious notices.
• An archaic, strong, authoritative tone; rarely used in everyday conversation.
• Often used with action verbs performed on the spot: 立ち入る, 撮影する, 喫煙する, 投棄する, 使用する.
fields.notes:
• On signs, “する” may be omitted: 喫煙べからず is also seen, but the standard is 喫煙するべからず.
• The structure is often written entirely in kanji for extra formality: 撮影禁止／撮影斯くの如し 等; however, べからず is still historically common.
• In classical literature/speeches, べからず can be used figuratively: 恐れるべからず (do not fear), but this usage is almost never seen in modern Japanese.
mistakes: Using it in conversation: × ここでタバコ吸うべからずよ → unnatural; use 吸わないでください/吸ってはいけません.
Wrong conjugation of a compound verb: × 立入るべからず → it should be 立ち入るべからず.
Confusing its nuance with べきではない (advice) → べからず is an absolute prohibition.

rows: <ruby>撮影<rt>さつえい</rt></ruby>するべからず。
<ruby>喫煙<rt>きつえん</rt></ruby>してはならない。
ここで<ruby>吸<rt>す</rt></ruby>うべきではない。

examples: A new system was introduced in order to raise productivity.
A questionnaire survey will be conducted in order to improve customer satisfaction.
I'm gathering information on scholarships in order to study abroad.
We stagger commuting hours in order to ease traffic congestion.
An event was planned with the aim of revitalizing the region.
He started keeping a diary in order to deepen his self-analysis.
fields.explain:
Puts the “purpose” at the beginning of the sentence: [Purpose] + べく、[Action]. Creates a formal, coherent style.
Not used with direct commands/requests: ×時間を守るべく、早く来てください → use ために/ように instead.
Not used when the two clauses have different subjects; with a different subject, use ために or ように.
Combines naturally with:実施する,取り組む,図る,導入する,開始する,強化する,設置する,改善する.

• Meaning: “To/in order to V; with the purpose of V”. Used before the main clause expressing an action aimed at achieving goal V.
• Formal nuance, often found in reports, news and planning documents: 〜すべく、〜を目指す/実施する/開始する/取り組む.
• Subject restriction: as a rule, the same agent carries out the purpose and the main action (like ために; unlike ように, which is used for goals of ability/results beyond one's control).
fields.notes:
• With サ変 nouns, “N + するべく/すべく” is very natural: 改善すべく, 検討すべく, 強化すべく.
• In headlines/plans, べく comes right after the goal: コスト削減すべく新体制へ.
• Chains of purpose: より良い社会を実現すべく、〜に取り組む/〜を推進する: common in policy writing.
mistakes: Using it when the subjects differ: × 学生を増やすべく、大学は奨学金が設けられた → use ために; or adjust the subjects so they match.
Using it for direct commands/requests: pragmatically inappropriate (use ために/ように/てもらう).
Confusing it with べくもない (there is no way…): this is a different pattern, not “purpose”.

rows: <ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>すべく<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する。
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>するために<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する。
Used for goals beyond one's control, often with なる/できる
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れないように<ruby>目覚<rt>めざ</rt></ruby>ましをかける。
<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>こるべくして<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>こった。
Idiom from なる + べく, a different meaning
